title: When the Winter Wakes
premise: August Almeida returns to the drowned village of Hollowmere to bury his twin sister, only to learn the coffin holds a stranger wearing her face. Fifteen years of rationalizing the house's noises collapse when the church bell—melted down in 1911—begins ringing a hymn whose final verse was never written down. The village's living residents are all singing it in their sleep, and each dawn one of them wakes as someone else entirely. August discovers his sister isn't dead but has been 'sung over' by the congregation, and that he was always meant to be the bell's new tongue. In the climax, on harvest moon night, August learns the last verse from his sister's stolen mouth, refuses to sing along, and instead sings the verse backward into the bell itself, shattering the cycle at the cost of every memory he has of her. He survives as a man who no longer knows why he came home, while the village sleeps soundly for the first time in a century.
about_author: Juniper Iversen is the pen name of a former church archivist who spent a decade cataloguing defunct parish records in coastal Scandinavia before turning to fiction. They write horror about small communities that keep their promises long after everyone who made them is gone.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: August arrives in Hollowmere to identify his twin sister Wren's body and finds a stranger's face beneath her name tag. POV: August. Emotional beat: disorientation and grief curdling into denial—he signs the paperwork anyway because leaving would mean admitting something is truly wrong.

chapters.title: A House That Remembers Him
chapters.summary: August stays in the childhood home, where objects sit exactly where fifteen-year-old Wren left them, including a half-finished letter addressed to him. POV: August. Emotional beat: uncanny comfort; the house seems to want him here, which should be a warning.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: teenage August cataloguing the house's noises—footsteps upstairs, humming in the walls—and building rational explanations with Wren's amused help. POV: August (past). Emotional beat: nostalgia shadowed by the realization that Wren never needed the explanations; she liked the noises.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: At the funeral, the melted-down church bell rings out across the village; only August and the gravedigger, old Mrs. Tarnow, react. Everyone else keeps singing the burial hymn mid-verse. POV: August. Emotional beat: first open fracture between him and reality—the explanations stop working.

chapters.title: The Congregation That Never Left
chapters.summary: August investigates the sealed church and finds pews worn smooth by use, hymnals open to a hymn with no last verse, and fresh candle wax. POV: August. Emotional beat: dread mixed with compulsion—he catches himself humming the tune and hates how well he knows it.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tarnow's Ledger
chapters.summary: The gravedigger shows August a century of burial records where names repeat every few decades, same faces, different dates—including an entry for 'Wren Almeida' dated 1911. POV: alternating August/Mrs. Tarnow. Emotional beat: loyalty tested; she begs him to leave before the harvest moon and he refuses to abandon the mystery of his sister.

chapters.title: Sleepers' Choir
chapters.summary: August walks the village at 3 a.m. and hears every house singing the hymn in unison through closed windows, each voice slightly wrong, layered like a recording of itself. POV: August. Emotional beat: isolation deepens—he is the only awake person in a dreaming town.

chapters.title: The First Replacement
chapters.summary: The baker's son wakes up as the baker—memories, mannerisms, wedding ring—and no one else notices, not even the wife. August alone sees the boy's terror behind the borrowed face. POV: August with a brief passage inside the boy's head. Emotional beat: horror becomes intimate; this could happen to anyone, to him.

chapters.title: What Wren Knew
chapters.summary: Searching Wren's room, August finds her research: the bell was cast from shipwreck iron in 1861, its last verse deliberately omitted because the verse is an instruction, and the congregation sings it to keep choosing who the bell takes. POV: August reading her notes in her voice. Emotional beat: grief reframes as betrayal—she knew and never told him.

chapters.title: The Verse Without Words
chapters.summary: August dreams the hymn and hears the missing verse wordlessly, waking with his lips moving and blood on them. The house's noises have stopped; the house is listening back. POV: August. Emotional beat: violation—the song is already inside him, learning his shape.

chapters.title: Invisible No Longer
chapters.summary: Villagers begin greeting August by name, warmly, insistently, inviting him to a 'rehearsal' at the church. His attempts to stay unnoticed end when the priest calls him 'the other twin' in front of everyone. POV: August. Emotional beat: paranoia peaks; invisibility, his lifelong strategy, is revoked.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: August attends under pretense and watches the congregation sing without breath, the priest conducting with a hand that casts no shadow. They leave a gap in the alto line exactly Wren's size. POV: August. Emotional beat: revulsion laced with longing—the music is beautiful and he hates himself for feeling it.

chapters.title: Tarnow's Last Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Tarnow reveals she was sung over once, in 1968, and clawed herself back out of a borrowed life; the price was forgetting her own daughter's face. She gives August the bell's original casting ledger. POV: Mrs. Tarnow primarily. Emotional beat: sorrowful solidarity—two people who refuse the song's mercy.

chapters.title: The Drowned Foundry
chapters.summary: Following the ledger, August wades into the flooded quarry where the bell was cast and finds the mold still standing underwater, warm, shaped like a person kneeling. Inside it, Wren's handwriting. POV: August. Emotional beat: hope and terror fused—his sister left him a message from somewhere the living shouldn't reach.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: Wren appears to August at dusk, whole and laughing, claiming she escaped the song and needs his help finishing the verse to free everyone. August wants desperately to believe her. POV: August. Emotional beat: love weaponized; the reader suspects what August cannot afford to.

chapters.title: The Trap of Mercy
chapters.summary: Mrs. Tarnow confronts 'Wren,' who recites memories only August and Wren shared—because the song took them from August's sleeping mind. August realizes his own memories are being harvested to bait him. POV: August. Emotional beat: heartbreak; the thing wearing his sister is built from his own best days.

chapters.title: Choosing Who the Bell Takes
chapters.summary: August breaks into the vestry and finds the congregation's true registry: a list of names in rotation, his own added in fresh ink, scheduled for the harvest moon. The priest catches him and explains, gently, that the song is the village's covenant—it keeps Hollowmere alive by feeding it people. POV: August and the priest. Emotional beat: moral vertigo—the horror believes it is a kindness.

chapters.title: What August Would Forget
chapters.summary: On the eve of the harvest moon, August writes down every memory of Wren he can bear to lose, understanding the backward verse will cost him all of them. Mrs. Tarnow helps him choose which ones to anchor with physical objects. POV: August. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness—grief rehearsed in advance.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: The village gathers in the churchyard under a swollen orange moon; the bell swings with no rope. The congregation begins the hymn, and the false Wren extends her hand to August, offering the last verse if he'll only sing along. POV: August. Emotional beat: terror at maximum—the moment of choice arrives dressed as reunion.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Backward
chapters.summary: August steps into the bell's shadow, takes the verse from the thing wearing his sister's mouth, and sings it reversed, syllable by syllable, while the congregation's song tears at his memories like hands stripping leaves. The bell cracks. POV: August, fragmenting. Emotional beat: triumphant self-destruction—he wins by giving up everything he came home to protect.

chapters.title: Morning Without Her
chapters.summary: August wakes in his car outside a silent village. The bell is rubble, the villagers wake ordinary and mortal, and Mrs. Tarnow remembers nothing of him. In his pocket: a list of memories in his handwriting, all of them blank now except one line—'you had a sister, and you chose right.' POV: August. Emotional beat: hollow victory; peace purchased with erasure.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Remember Learning
chapters.summary: Driving away, August stops at a crossroads chapel where an old hymnal lies open, and finds himself humming a tune he doesn't know, stopping just before a verse he somehow knows is last. He closes the book and drives on. POV: August. Emotional beat: ambiguous coda—the song sleeps, but songs wait; loyalty outlives memory after all.
